articles.title_orig: A 7.0 earthquake hits China’s Tibet, killing 16 and injuring 32
articles.title_zh: A 7.0 earthquake hits China’s Tibet, killing 16 and injuring 32
articles.content_orig:
More than 300 houses have collapsed, and disaster relief work continues
At least 16 people were killed and 32 more injured when a strong 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck China’s western Tibet autonomous region late on Thursday, state news agency Xinhua said, citing local authorities.
More than 300 houses collapsed in the earthquake, which struck on Thursday at 10.33pm. Officials were still evaluating the damage, and disaster relief work was ongoing, Xinhua said.
The epicentre of the quake was located in a mountainous area about 190km (120 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu and 390km northeast of the regional capital Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said.
It struck at a shallow depth of 10km (6 miles) in Maru township in Baqen county.

Stocks mostly slid Thursday on renewed concerns around spending by artificial intelligence companies, while oil prices jumped amid rising geopolitical tensions.
The Nasdaq Composite pulled back 2.6% to 26,008.86, while the S&P 500 shed 1.21% to close at 7,663.43. The tech-heavy index suffered its worst session since June, while the S&P 500 posted its worst daily performance since July. The Dow Jones Industrial Average inched up 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to end at 52,867.98.
Meta Platforms slipped about 7%, even as it exceeded revenue expectations and offered upbeat guidance. Technology more broadly was under pressure as well as ongoing concerns about artificial intelligence spending persisted. Advanced Micro Devices fell more than 8%, while Micron Technology and Nvidia dropped 6% and 4%, respectively.
Neocloud leader CoreWeave , whose bond yields and credit default swaps remained elevated , declined 10% as well. The move comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ." However, he added that capital is scarce and impeding growth.
Huang's commentary about a scarcity of capital is "spooking markets and reigniting the concerns around the capital markets on the credit side being full from a risk appetite standpoint," said Wells Fargo traders in a note. They also said Meta's comments about the large amount of AI funding needed caused the shares to roll over and weighed on the overall market.
JPMorgan traders noted that Wednesday's bullish "tone reversed overnight" because Meta shares rolled over in the premarket and chatter increased "over renewed Iran kinetic-risk post US mid-term election."
Additionally, "underlying price actions and feedback from our trading desk also suggested the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction/re-grossing from the recent tech reversal," they said in a note to clients.
Oil prices, meanwhile, jumped after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections. President Donald Trump also told reporters late Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Tehran and that something will happen "fairly soon."
International benchmark Brent crude futures rose 4% to settle at $113.17 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude futures advanced 2.39% to $99.47 per barrel.
Investors also turned to U.S. Treasurys in their search for a safe haven. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, falling to its lowest level in almost a month . The 2-year note yield also shed more than 16 basis points to 4.659%.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite saw sizable declines on Thursday.
The broad market index moved down 1.21% to 7,663.43, while the tech-heavy index decreased 2.6% to 26,008.86.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, however, traded just above the flatline, rising 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to 52,867.98.
Shares of power and energy companies tied to the AI boom plunged Thursday as investors grew increasingly concerned about the soaring costs of data center expansion.
Two major energy equipment players, GE Vernova and Bloom Energy , led the declines, with each falling more than 11%. As investors sold their AI infrastructure stocks, Vistra also shed over 10%, while Quanta Services dropped more than 8%. Talen Energy and Eaton declined 8.3% and nearly 7%, respectively.
The selloff came as Meta's latest earnings report reignited concerns over AI infrastructure spending. The tech giant raised its capital expenditure forecast, highlighting the enormous investment required to support its AI ambitions and raising questions about how quickly those investments will generate returns.
Nuclear energy stocks were also caught in the downturn, with Oklo falling more than 4% and NuScale Power declining over 3%. The broad retreat shows a deeper, growing investor unease over whether the pace of AI infrastructure investment is sustainable.
Oil prices spiked Thursday as investors fear escalation in the Middle East with the U.S. reportedly planning to resume strikes against Iran.
Brent crude futures gained 4% to close at $113.17 per barrel, the highest level for the international benchmark since May 4. U.S. West Texas Intermediate gained 2.4% to settle at $99.47.

articles.title_orig: Trump signs housing affordability executive order
articles.title_zh: Trump signs housing affordability executive order
articles.content_orig:
The White House is considering ordering Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and multiple federal agencies to implement a raft of policy changes aimed at lowering mortgage financing costs ahead of upcoming midterm elections, according to a draft executive order obtained by Scotsman Guide.
The proposed order would direct the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) — which oversee government-guaranteed mortgage programs — to unliterally lower mortgage rates on single-family loans using agency authorities.
Fannie and Freddie, according to the draft order, would also be directed to review their portfolios for borrowers eligible to have their mortgage insurance “cancelled proactively,” in keeping with safety and soundness expectations, their contractual obligations and growing collateral risks .
Mortgage servicers thus could be mandated by Fannie and Freddie, “to the extent permitted by law and operationally feasible, to notify borrowers promptly when mortgage insurance may be cancelled” and reduce and eliminate “unnecessary documentation requests, appraisal costs, and other administrative barriers to cancellation.”
The draft order reviewed by Scotsman Guide is subject to change — or may not be issued at all — but multiple industry sources who have seen the document said it may be issued by the White House as soon as Wednesday.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
Organized into five sections and containing a multitude of provisions , the draft executive order is titled “Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People.” It is unclear whether the range of directives in the order comply with existing mortgage laws and authorities of relevant federal agencies.
“Over the past two decades, many creditworthy Americans have been locked out of homeownership due to the rising costs associated with homeownership,” the draft order states as its purpose, citing “unnecessary” regulatory requirements and “outdated” origination processes that have increased closing costs and “made homeownership unaffordable.”
Just weeks out from hotly contested November midterm elections, Republican lawmakers in the Senate and House of Representatives are struggling to carry their water with voters as surveys favor Democrats to win back both chambers of Congress. Costs of living are voters’ primary concern , as they were during the presidential election in 2024 when Republicans won the White House and took control of both the House and Senate.
Perhaps nowhere are ongoing homebuying affordability challenges more visible than in mortgage rates now averaging more than 7%, compared to rates of around 6% in February. Elevated borrowing costs have amplified mortgage rate lock-in effects, given that two-thirds of existing borrowers have loans with rates under 5%.
Not only have elevated borrowing costs sidelined prospective buyers and slowed housing turnover to multidecade lows, but higher rates have also sapped the market of refinance demand .
Many borrowers have stretched their budgets in recent years to purchase a home at elevated mortgage rates — with the intention of lowering their monthly payments by refinancing when rates drop. But rates have only steadily risen since March and are projected to spend all of 2027 around current levels, according to economists at Fannie Mae and the Mortgage Bankers Association.
The draft order would authorize Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director Bill Pulte to consider significant expansion of a title insurance waiver pilot program for eligible refinances, with the aim of lowering closing costs on refinances in a range of new ways.
The FHFA did not respond to Scotsman Guide’s request for comment.
The title waiver pilot program began in 2024 and allowed for alternative title verification methods on certain refinance transactions. That includes removing geographic limitations, widening eligibility to borrowers with less than 20% equity and “certifying additional title-assessment providers to promote competition.”
The draft order also proposes “reducing or eliminating loan-level price adjustments” for eligible refinances and “waiving appraisals, income re-verification, and other documentation requirements for limited cash-out refinances that reduce the borrower’s monthly payment, where the Enterprise’s existing data support doing so.”
In lieu of appraisals, the order suggests Fannie and Freddie would “embrace innovative risk and value assessment technologies that incorporate Super Intelligence to drive down mortgage and homeownership costs,” using President Donald Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence.
“The Director shall require that cost savings resulting from the program be passed through to borrowers and that lenders inform borrowers of those savings,” the draft order states.
Taking a page out of Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s book, one section of the draft order would direct the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Department of Commerce, VA and USDA to start a “task force” to standardize permitting and facilitate production of manufactured and factory-built housing.
That task force, which would be co-chaired by Pulte and HUD Secretary Scott Turner, would also evaluate under what existing laws federal grant funding “may be conditioned” on adoption of standardized permitting and licensing for factory-built housing at the state and local levels.
Eric Souza contributed reporting.
Ryan Kingsley is a senior staff writer at Scotsman Guide.

articles.title_orig: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
articles.title_zh: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
articles.content_orig:
In case there were any doubts, Mark Zuckerberg is staying in California.
Meta was apparently concerned enough that its founder and CEO might depart its home state that the company put in place a new stock plan that could help offset the burden of higher taxes should a billionaires tax, known as Proposition 40, pass on Election Day on Nov. 3.
The disclosure came in a filing on Wednesday that coincided with Meta's third-quarter earnings report, and represents a first among California's megacap tech companies. Zuckerberg, the sixth-richest person in the world, is one of the few among his peers to still reside in the state, along with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .
Elon Musk and Michael Dell live in Texas, while Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' primary residence has always been elsewhere. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin moved out of California ahead of the election and bought luxury homes in Florida, the same state that Oracle founder Larry Ellison officially calls home.
Prop. 40 would impose a 5% tax on Californians worth over $1 billion. Zuckerberg's net worth is currently about $225 billion.
"If the California wealth tax is enacted and Mr. Zuckerberg becomes liable for a tax payment, Mr. Zuckerberg would effectively be paying to serve as the Company's chief executive officer while residing in California," the filing said, noting the CEO's "salary of only $1 each year."
Meta said in the filing that Zuckerberg committed to remaining in California for eight years, "unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."
The company created a new class of non-voting Class C common stock to take effect in January. Zuckerberg will essentially be granted a portion of the new stock via a dividend. He will be able to "immediately sell or transfer up to 20%" of the shares he's granted "for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control," the filing said.
The tech industry, by and large, has been unified in its objection to the ballot measure.
In addition to the Google co-founders, a number of big-name techies have put spending into opposing Prop. 40. They include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, venture investor Peter Thiel and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, according to various media reports based on campaign filings.
Collison and Xu are members of Meta's board of directors while Thiel left the company's board in 2022, having served since 2005.
Brin told The New York Times in April he fled the Soviet Union with his family in 1979, and said "I don't want California to end up in the same place."
Huang, however, recently told CBS Sunday Morning that it would be a "privilege" to pay the tax. Huang is just behind Zuckerberg in Forbes' billionaire ranking , with a net worth of $185 billion.
Although Prop. 40 advocates, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., have been urging voters to pass the ballot measure , recent polling has suggested that it may fail to garner the majority support required to make it law. A recent Citrin-Politico poll showed 46% are in favor of the measure compared to 43% who oppose it.
Meta, with the help of a special committee, views Zuckerberg as key to the company's future and its efforts to become a major player in artificial intelligence, according to the filing. In particular, the company said it doesn't want to jeopardize Zuckerberg's close working arrangement with the Meta Superintelligence Labs , which is led by AI chief Alexandr Wang .
"The Special Committee believes that Mr. Zuckerberg's talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the Special Committee wants that to continue," the filing said.
Although Meta considered the possibility of issuing Class A common stock to help raise funds, the filing noted that Zuckerberg made clear "that he would not support a significant equity financing that would have the effect of reducing his voting power in the Company."
Doing so will help Meta receive "critical equity capital without impacting Mr. Zuckerberg's voting power and the unique and creative vision and exceptional management abilities which helped to deliver the long-term value as noted above," the filing said.

Beijing offers to remove restrictions on a German supplier to chipmaking giant ASML in exchange for the EU delisting Chinese firm Yusha
Diplomats from the EU’s 27 member states were pressured this week to lift sanctions on Yusha Group, a Chinese textiles manufacturer accused of selling sensitive European technology to Russian buyers.
In exchange, Beijing has pledged that the company will refrain from shipping banned items to Russian military-linked buyers. It will also remove German company Sindlhauser Materials from its own export controls list, according to multiple sources familiar with the affair.
The unusual quid pro quo – the product of high-wire negotiations at the top level of EU and Chinese politics – is designed to protect the supply chain of Europe’s most valuable technology company, Dutch-based ASML, of which Sindlhauser is a reported supplier.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls more than 2% for worst day since June as AI spending woes, oil prices spark sell-off: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls more than 2% for worst day since June as AI spending woes, oil prices spark sell-off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slid sharply on Thursday amid mounting concerns over whether massive investments in artificial intelligence will pay off and high oil prices.
Shortly before the close of trading, the Nasdaq Composite Index, where many technology companies exposed to AI are listed, tumbled 751 points, or 2.8%, before rebounding slightly to close 694 points lower at 26,009. The broader S&P 500 fell 1.2%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average eked out a small gain of less than 0.1%.
Investors are increasingly worried about the enormous debt AI companies are taking on to finance data center spending and whether the companies will generate the profits investors are banking on, according to Wall Street analysts.
"AI growth is dependent on capex (this is one of the most capital-intensive industries ever), and since capex is dramatically outpacing op. cash flow, companies are reliant on the largess of equity and debt investors to underwrite all the spending, but lately those markets are becoming increasingly less accommodating," Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note to investors on Thursday.
Slowing debt issuance as the credit environment tightens could hinder companies' ability to finance the AI infrastructure buildout, Crisafulli added.
The Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan think tank, estimates that it will cost more than $10 trillion to develop AI infrastructure between 2025 and 2032. That would amount to the largest tide of investment in U.S. history, dwarfing the construction of the railroads in the 19th century and, more recently, the dot-com boom, according to Carl Weinberg, chief economist for the financial market analysis firm High Frequency Economics.
Although many of the big players driving the AI boom remain highly profitable, investors are reassessing those massive costs as their stock prices soar.
The drop in markets on Thursday came amid a series of earnings reports that showed mixed performance results. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent , lost 7% after revenue topped estimates while profit fell short. Tesla slipped 3.1%, with the electric vehicle company reporting stronger-than-expected summer profits but weaker revenue than analysts expected.
A rise in oil prices, driven by concerns about escalations in the war in Iran, was also weighing on stocks on Thursday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $99.21 a barrel, up 2.1%, while Brent crude, the international standard, was trading at around $113 a barrel, up 3.7%.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Russian missiles pound Kyiv as Moscow says over 800 Ukrainian drones downed
articles.title_zh: Russian missiles pound Kyiv as Moscow says over 800 Ukrainian drones downed
articles.content_orig:
Estimated read time: 5-6 minutes
KYIV, Ukraine — Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles in an hourslong nighttime barrage, while the Russian military said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted over 800 drones fired by Ukraine at Moscow and other cities.
At least four people were killed in Ukraine and dozens of others were wounded, officials said, in the attacks that began only hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed "in principle" on Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations between Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
"Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after the latest large-scale barrage.
Putin's consent came in talks in St. Petersburg with President Donald Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff, who had spoken of a "new momentum" toward peace after meeting Tuesday with Zelenskyy in Norway. No date was set for the tripartite talks.
Representatives of the three countries held rounds of "technical" talks in the United Arab Emirates and Switzerland in January and February, seeking to lay the groundwork for detailed negotiations. But they reported little progress beyond exchanges of prisoners of war. Russia and Ukraine remain far apart in their terms for stopping the fighting despite U.S. efforts.
Zelenskyy says only a meeting of leaders can end the deadlock.
Russia's aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine overnight, killing at least four people and wounding scores of others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday.
Two women aged 50 and 60 were killed and dozens of others wounded in a Russian strike on a market in Lozova, in Ukraine's northeastern Kharkiv region, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration. Another person was killed in other strikes on Kharkiv, the State Emergency Service said.
The Ukrainian capital endured a noisy night as 21 ballistic missiles came in three waves, Zelenskyy said, smashing apartment buildings, energy facilities, a railway station and the Kyiv subway system, shopping malls and businesses. One person was killed in Kyiv.
The Russian attack on Kyiv included three ballistic missiles carrying cluster munitions — bombs that open in the air and release scores of smaller bomblets, Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainians are bracing for the bitterly cold months ahead as the recent escalation in Russian attacks targets the power grid to deny civilians heat, light and running water. Ukraine says Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for an annual campaign Ukrainians describe as "weaponizing winter."
Since Oct. 11, Russia has launched 170 strikes on Ukraine's critical energy facilities, Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader has pleaded with Washington to supply more Patriot air defense ammunition to stop the ballistic missiles, and to heap more sanctions on Russia to pressure Moscow to pursue peace.
Instead, Trump has agreed with Putin to import diesel from Russia and waived heavy sanctions on Moscow, while U.S. officials say Patriot ammunition is in short supply.
"Russia is clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defense supplies from our partners," Zelenskyy said. "It is equally clear that when some partners ease the pressure on Russia, it only reinforces Putin's belief that his goals are within reach."
Western analysts say Putin wants to cut out Europe and Kyiv and negotiate Ukraine's future directly with Washington. The Trump administration has also disparaged Europe.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Putin had received an invitation to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December but hasn't yet decided whether to go.
"The American administration is doing a lot to help a peaceful settlement," Peskov told reporters. "European capitals are doing nothing to promote a peaceful resolution, and they are doing a great deal to provoke the further escalation of fighting."
Witkoff, the Trump envoy who met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, was harshly criticized in Ukraine and in the U.S. for praising the Russian leader as a "humanitarian" for ordering the release of a retired American teacher who was imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
Assassination attempts against Putin's foes — routinely denied by the Kremlin — have been common during his decades in power. And as the five-year anniversary of Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor approaches, aerial strikes have killed thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of soldiers.
The latest "brutal" Russian attacks demonstrate "what Russian 'humanism' truly sounds like," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. "Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will."
Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses overnight downed 808 Ukrainian drones, with two people reported wounded.
Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 630 of the drones were fired toward the Russian capital between late Wednesday and early Thursday. Moscow airports temporarily restricted air traffic overnight.
The Russian military hit the facilities involved in making and storing drones and cruise missiles and transport infrastructure in Kyiv in overnight strikes, the Defense Ministry said. Infrastructure in the southern port of Odesa and vessels used for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it said.
In other developments, the bodies of 252 people, said by Russia to be Ukrainian soldiers, were returned to Ukraine in an exchange, Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said Thursday.
Russia received 25 bodies of Russian soldiers, Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliyev, a member of a parliamentary coordination group overseeing the exchanges, told the RBC news outlet.

Airbnb is updating its rules to shield visitors from onerous cleaning tasks it says could negatively impact their stay.
The new policy, announced this week, prevents hosts from asking guests to strip beds, start a load of laundry and other household chores Airbnb says "require significant effort or time" and would typically be performed by a cleaner.
These tasks could lead guests to write negative reviews, Airbnb said, which ultimately hurt the property owner.
The new policy sparked backlash among some hosts, with more than 5,000 people signing a Change.org petition calling on Airbnb to reverse the rules. The signatories argued that the policy goes too far and is "unreasonable."
Requiring a cleaner to pick up the slack could hike expenses for hosts, which could ultimately be passed on to guests in the form of higher accommodation prices, the petition says.
"These are not professional cleaning duties," the petition says. "They are ordinary aspects of living responsibly in somebody else's property."
The online booking platform clarified which requests are "reasonable" as part of a new policy it unveiled on its website . The new rules apply to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20, according to Airbnb.
In some cases, it's a fine line: hosts can ask guests to put used dishes in the sink, but they can't ask them to wash or put away dishes. They can request that guests separate trash and recycling, but can't ask guests to deposit garbage at an off-site facility.
"When adding a request, remember that most guests want to avoid unexpected chores," Airbnb said on its website.
Airbnb said that if hosts repeatedly violate the rules, the rental company could reduce the visibility of their listing page or issue a notice to guests on the listing page about the host's violation.

articles.title_zh: U.S. 10-Year Treasury Yield Falls Under 5% as French Turmoil Fuels Flight for Safety
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."
Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.
"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."
The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that while demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are a specialized cloud computing providers that focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.
This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.
Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.
Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.
Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."
"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Taco Bell sticks with Pepsi as sister chain switches to Coke
articles.title_zh: Taco Bell sticks with Pepsi as sister chain switches to Coke
articles.content_orig:
IRVINE, Calif. — KFC dumped PepsiCo last week, but its sister chain Taco Bell announced Thursday it's keeping the Mountain Dew Baja Blast maker on for another decade.
The Taco Bell deal is a much-needed win for PepsiCo, whose business has had rough few weeks. Not only did it lose its longstanding contract with KFC to rival Coca-Cola , but its drink business in North America is also in a slump.
The company reported a 2% decline for its North America beverage unit during its most recent quarter, and its CEO Ramon Laguarta bluntly said on its earnings call that it's "not competing well in soft drinks," including newly acquired Poppi brand.
Losing the KFC contract is a blow for PepsiCo, considering it once owned the fried chicken chain. But keeping Taco Bell is a bigger deal, since the latter has generated $17 billion in U.S. systemwide sales last year compared to KFC's roughly $5 billion. (Both chains are owned by Yum! Brands.)
Taco Bell and PepsiCo said in a statement that the two will continue collaborating on new beverages and foods until 2036, including upcoming new flavors for their Doritos Locos Tacos. It also noted that the Baja Blast drink has become a $1 billion brand.
As food prices rise and consumers look to cut back, the beverage category is a key growth area for Taco Bell and other fast food chains.
Taco Bell is aggressively expanding its beverage sales aiming to generate $5 billion in revenue by 2030. Last year, the chain released a lineup of "Refrescas" drinks aimed at attracting consumers searching for a beverage between meals. Further expansion will come from developing new Baja Blast options with Pepsi, including a limited-time pink lemonade with singer Olivia Rodrigo.
"Taco Bell's Baja Blast lineup has often been a key differentiator for the brand, and leaning into product exclusives can help drive visitation to quick service restaurant chains," Elizabeth Lafontaine, director of research at location analytics firm Placer.ai, previously told CNN.
"Especially as the industry faces steeper competition and consumers who are on the hunt for more value from fast food offerings," she added.
Taco Bell and PepsiCo said in a statement that they plan to stay ahead on "emerging beverage trends across crafted, functional and energy beverages, including energy offerings designed to appeal to Gen Z consumers and unlock new morning and afternoon occasions."
Taco Bell has been a bright spot in the fast food industry, but saw a traffic decline over the summer due to a cyclosporasis outbreak that was linked to lettuce served at a number of restaurants. The company will give a fuller view of the sales impact when it releases earnings next month.

articles.title_zh: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots
articles.content_orig:
Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend.
The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected.
France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.
France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.
Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.
Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.
Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la République, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday.
Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city.
The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses.
The prefecture for the Rhône region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT).
Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.
"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced.
"When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests .
Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Mark Zuckerberg made a deal with Meta's board to help him pay a proposed California tax on billionaires without losing his ownership stake in the company he founded, according to regulatory filings published this week.
The wealth tax is before California voters in the election that concludes Nov. 3. If passed, the measure would levy a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Zuckerberg is the sixth-richest person in the world with a net worth estimated at more than $220 billion, according to Forbes. That would put his tax liability at more than $11 billion.
Actions announced by the tech giant on Wednesday will keep Zuckerberg as the majority owner of the company -- and also give him the ability to sell some of a new class of non-voting shares "for any reason," including to pay potential bills from the wealth tax .
The compromise came after Zuckerberg told the board he was considering selling his Palo Alto home last month in anticipation of the proposed tax. But he later struck the deal and committed to staying in California for eight years, unless "material unforeseen circumstances" arise that make it "prudent or advisable for him to reside elsewhere," according to the filings.
Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the deal.
A few hundred billionaires live in California, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office. The tax would apply to anyone with a primary residence in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Most of the money would be used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% of it would go toward education and food-assistance programs. Proponents, including SEIU United Healthcare Workers West and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, say it will help ensure the ultra-rich pay their fair share.
But opponents, including Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, have warned it could prompt the state's wealthiest to leave the state. That could cause budget problems down the line because the state relies heavily on the rich for income tax revenue.
SEIU United Healthcare Workers West said the Zuckerberg deal proves them wrong.
"This is the nail in the coffin to months of scare tactics claiming that billionaires are fleeing California," Suzanne Jimenez, the union's chief of staff, said in a statement.
Zuckerberg's deal with Meta offers a glimpse into how the ultrawealthy may be bracing for the tax, which targets the main way they make money — through their investments, instead of by raising taxes on the paycheck they receive from work. Other billionaires have taken a different approach by starting to cut ties with the state, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page.
Brin and other tech moguls and venture capitalists have poured millions into a political committee opposing the wealth tax proposal and backing other ballot measures designed to nullify it. The committee, Building a Better California, has raised more than $333 million, 30% of which has come from Brin. By comparison, the "Yes on 40" campaign has raised $32.7 million.
Beyond securing Zuckerberg's future in California, Meta's new class of nonvoting shares is intended to boost the company's ability to raise capital for its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to the filings.
Zuckerberg has taken a salary of $1 each year as Meta's CEO since 2013. In its regulatory filings, Meta maintained that he would not receive additional compensation — and argued that Zuckerberg would "effectively be paying to serve as the Company's chief executive officer while residing in California" if the state's wealth tax is enacted. The company said the new stock he will be allowed to sell (representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company) will help mitigate that.
Grantham-Philips reported from Chicago.

Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up.
Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.
The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.
1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.
“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”
Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.
This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.
Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company .
TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.
Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.
“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”
Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.
In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.
Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.
Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.
The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan , a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”
Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.
Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”
As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

BAB EL-MANDEB, Yemen — To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world’s most vital waterways.
The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that’s become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
“You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you’d think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money,” said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals.
“So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you,” he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach.
Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia.
But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast .
The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the “Gate of Tears” for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen’s coast and Djibouti and Eritrea.
About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island , which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait’s narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease.
“We don’t need a drone or a missile,” one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim’s coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait.
The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn’t be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal’s southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs.
A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods.
More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group.
These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran  prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz —  cutting off the world’s most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb.
That’s especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it’s also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat.
The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce.
But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa‘s airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom.
The rebels’ land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help.
Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement.” He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them.
“They don’t want to attract international military operations,” said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory.
“They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world.”
But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of “every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation.”
Using tribal power and rigorous detective work, a family of an army officer in Yemen tries to find out how he was abducted in broad daylight, and what happened to him afterward.
In the meantime, the Houthis have been consolidating their gains on Yemen’s coast, Basha said, setting up checkpoints and bringing loyalists to administer the regions now under their control.
In taking the coastal areas around Bab el-Mandeb village, they reap the benefit of Emirati investment, manifested in kilometers of paved highways that stand in stark contrast to much of Yemen’s road network. They also gain control of several airbases in the area, most crucially on Perim, where the Emirates spent years ferrying construction supplies to build out a roughly 6,000-foot runway along with three hangars.
Although such a runway could not be used by larger bombers, it still can accommodate attack and surveillance aircraft. Another area of the island, which lies roughly two miles off of Yemen’s coast, has what appears to be a helicopter landing area.
The U.S.-Israel campaign against Iran was billed as the final blow to Tehran’s ‘Axis of Resistance,’ but the alliance though bloodied is unexpectedly resilient.
One resident in Bab el-Mandeb village said much of that construction was done by the Emirates, whose contractors would ferry Southeast Asian construction workers to the island and provide them with food. It also built roughly 100 structures for Perim’s residents.

The company saw strong growth in facilities management and critical infrastructure services, executives said Thursday, but project management growth dipped as corporations cut real estate spending.
CBRE’s revenue grew 13% year over year to $11.5 billion, the company reported . On a net revenue basis, its project management business grew 11%, driven in part by growth in infrastructure projects. That segment “is a very large part of our project management business [and] more than [offsets] the slowdown in real estate,” Giamartino said.
CBRE’s critical infrastructure services business — which includes network infrastructure, mechanical, engineering and plumbing projects and facilities management for data centers — is expected to generate nearly $4.5 billion of revenue in 2027, according to Sulentic.
Its acquisition of a global IT infrastructure company, Onnec Group Limited, will help drive the growth, said Sulentic, adding that even if data center growth in the U.S. eases, growth is expected to increase in other countries.
“Our acquisition of Onnec, which we announced today, fits within this line of business,” Sulentic said.
The $610 million cash deal provides CBRE with technical capabilities related to design, deployment and maintenance of network, fiber and data center infrastructure, a specialty area that’s critical to data centers, per a release Tuesday .
If the business achieves the entirety of the deal’s earn-outs, the deal will end up costing CBRE a little over $1 billion, which the firm is using as an incentive to continue to generate strong growth, Giamartino said.
The firm expects to close the acquisition by the end of the year, said Giamartino, noting that if the acquisition were included, the firm’s critical infrastructure services business would have generated approximately $3 billion in revenue over the past 12 months.
Although the company’s enterprise facilities management posted solid growth, it’s facing pressure from a handful of problematic accounts. “That’s happened from time to time over the years,” Sulentic said. “The market gets frothy, it gets more and more competitive and you … end up with some broker hires or outsourcing or enterprise accounts that don’t have the characteristics you would want.”
CBRE’s project management revenue slowed, up 3% year over year, as corporate clients acted more conservatively due to uncertainty in the economy, Sulentic said.
“We do a lot of work for big tech clients that have moved their spending away from … traditional legacy real estate-type investment into infrastructure, critical infrastructure, data centers,” he said. “I think you’re seeing some of that.” The firm also saw “a little bit of concentration slowdown in healthcare,” he said.
“What we really need is for rates to stabilize,” Giamartino said. “The volatility and the uncertainty is what’s driving a pause or a hold or even delaying deals to 2027. We expect that stability to come in the back half of next year….  Of course, if that doesn’t come or things change, the results will be different.”
In the U.S., leasing revenue rose 4%, supported by industrial, which was up 16%,  while office leasing dipped 2%, Giamartino said.
This dip, which contrasts with a broader office recovery occurring in the market, is the result of some big deals that slipped into Q4, “which is in part why we have confidence that we’ll see double-digit growth in leasing in Q4.,” she said.
Despite the cautious economic outlook, Sulentic believes that even if things slow down in the U.S. — either because of the interest rate or political environment — CBRE believes growth will accelerate globally, especially in the data center sector.
“Onnec puts us in a great position to take care of that,” Sulentic said. Even if data center growth slows in the U.S., there should be plenty of business involving existing facilities. “We think that in data centers, you’re going to see potentially some pressure on the amount of new build,” he said. “And then what’s happening, and we’re already seeing it, is a lot of refit of existing data centers.”
Outside of its critical infrastructure business, CBRE’s infrastructure services work consists of overseeing the construction of transportation and energy assets along with data centers within project management, as well as sales, leasing and financing for data centers and advisory services. When taking this work into account, CBRE expects its total infrastructure services revenue to spike 40% from this year to $7 billion in 2027, Sulentic said.

articles.content_orig:
With no more polls allowed to be released before the election, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is reaching the 61-seats necessary for an outright majority
ack GUEZ / AFP via Getty Images
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (R) of the Likud party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026.
The likeliest outcome of Israel’s upcoming election is a stalemate , according to the final polls ahead of next Tuesday’s election, with neither side — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the bloc opposing him, led by Gadi Eisenkot — projected to reach a majority of the Knesset.
Israeli law prohibits the publication of new polls from Friday until the Oct. 27 election.
The overall polling average put the bloc led by Netanyahu ahead, with 54 seats, while the opposition would get 50 seats, both short of the necessary 61-seat majority. Netanyahu’s Likud polled at 23 seats compared to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party.
However, the gap between polls from right-leaning news outlets and those from the mainstream networks and publications was significant.
In the average of six mainstream TV and newspaper polls, the Eisenkot-led bloc had more seats than the current coalition. An average of polls from the last two days showed Eisenkot’s bloc narrowly ahead, holding 52 seats to the Netanyahu bloc’s 50 seats.
Meanwhile, an average of the polls on Israel’s Channel 14 and i24 News, which use pollsters who had previously worked for Likud, found Netanyahu’s coalition projected to receive a 61-seat majority of the Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc would only have 45 seats.
The Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, are polling at an average of 14 seats, just short of their record 15 seats in 2020 when they ran together.
Arab voter turnout has hovered around the 50% mark in the last decade. However, Stat-Net, a polling institute specializing in the Israeli Arab population, has said that it may be as high as 68-69% this year, which may give the parties representing the Arab minority even more seats than projected.
Increased Arab turnout would contribute to higher overall turnout, which would increase the number of votes needed to meet the minimal threshold to enter the Knesset.
In both the general polling average and the right-leaning media’s polls, neither Amcha Yisrael nor the Reservists and Economy Party, which have hovered near the 3.25% electoral threshold in recent weeks, received enough votes to enter the Knesset. In the more left-leaning polls, Reservists and Economy, which has not pledged to recommend either Netanyahu or Eisenkot for prime minister, receives an average of three seats.

articles.title_orig: Moderna shares plunge after leak of cancer vaccine data despite positive results
articles.title_zh: Moderna shares plunge after leak of cancer vaccine data despite positive results
articles.content_orig:
Moderna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its closely watched cancer vaccine developed with Merck .
Shares of both drugmakers fell even though the data, released in full later Thursday following the leak, appeared meaningful for patients and positive relative to Wall Street expectations.
The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone.
The data also showed that the shot along with Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy.
The companies said about 82% of patients who received the personalized cancer vaccine alongside Keytruda were alive without their melanoma returning at two years after receiving the shot, compared with 70% of those who received Keytruda alone.
"This is a huge development for our patients," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD ​Anderson Cancer Center, about the results.
He said that the added benefit of the vaccine also comes with much milder toxicity, or side effects like injection-site pain, compared to other cancer treatments.
The detailed phase 3 trial results were set to be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference this weekend.
"Whenever you put a therapy on top of something that works really well, like Keytruda, sometimes it's harder to show additional benefit. We have no problems of showing additional benefit here," Dr. Dean Li, Merck Research Laboratories president, said in an interview ahead of the results.
The benefit appeared even larger after the six-month vaccine regimen, with a separate analysis showing a 58% reduction in risk of recurrence or death. The companies say it is still too early to determine whether the treatment helps patients live longer overall.
Several analysts acknowledged investors' elevated expectations ahead of the release, but noted that the data is overall positive.
"We assert this relative reduction in recurrence/death is clinically meaningful," BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman said in a research note on Thursday following the leak. "Such a [stock] reaction likely reflects inflated expectations into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy."
Oncologists and investors see the targeted vaccine as a possible breakthrough treatment, with the potential to be used to treat other forms of cancer in the future. Merck and Moderna are studying the vaccine in several trials across other tumors, such as non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
But Li acknowledged the companies have more work to show the product can be effective across tumor types.
"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Li said. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
The shot is designed to target the specific mutations in each patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach. The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Keytruda, which helps the body attack the cancer more effectively.
It could also offer Moderna a critical additional commercial product in its pipeline, following vaccines for Covid-19, the flu and respiratory syncytial virus.
In a research note Thursday, UBS analysts said "this is overall a strong data set" and gives more confidence in upcoming studies of the vaccine in kidney and bladder cancers. They added the stock reaction may be due more to massive expectations than disappointing data.
Against the backdrop of those high expectations, Moderna shares have spiked more than 530% year-to-date as of Thursday afternoon.
Shares of Merck, a much larger drugmaker, fell by about 1% on Thursday. The company's stock has climbed nearly 41% this year.
Since the vaccine is personalized, the complicated manufacturing process can take six weeks. But Merck CEO Robert Davis told CNBC last week that the company believes it can shorten that timeline in the future, potentially allowing the shot to reach more patients more quickly.

articles.title_zh: Markets tumble as concerns about Iran war and high AI spending collide
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the United States would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold on to recent gains.
The S&P 500 closed down 1.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 2.6%. The price of international Brent crude climbed nearly 4% to $113 a barrel, its highest level since May, while U.S. crude gained more than 2% to close at more than $99 a barrel.
Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the past several weeks — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets amid riskier ones like tech stocks selling off. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell below 5% for the first time since late September.
The market moves were sparked in part by reports that Israel and the U.S. were preparing for a military operation in Iran after the November midterm elections.
Likely targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to The New York Times .
U.S. military and diplomatic personnel were also being evacuated from several countries in the Middle East, NBC News reported.
Iranian officials have promised widespread retaliation to any strikes, pointing to critical Middle East data center sites and undersea internet cables as potential targets.
“It’s been another difficult 24 hours for markets, as investors grapple with AI growth concerns, higher oil prices, and ongoing fiscal stress,” Henry Allen, director and macro strategist at Deutsche Bank, wrote in a note to clients Thursday.
Major tech stocks led the declines in equity markets, with Meta and Tesla dropping after both companies reported quarterly earnings Wednesday.
Meta’s earnings and revenues beat forecasts, but only after excluding billions of dollars in legal penalties the company paid last quarter. It also warned investors that it expects to increase its spending in the coming year to meet demands for computing power.
A separate regulatory filing revealed that Meta intends to spend an additional $825 billion on contracts related to its AI infrastructure build-out.
Tesla, meanwhile, said it was reining in its capital spending plans, disappointing investors who were hoping for a signal of more aggressive expansion.
The slide in the Nasdaq got additional fuel Thursday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an appearance on CNBC that capital to finance the AI investment boom was becoming “scarce” due to higher interest rates and a glut of existing spending commitments.
Despite Thursday’s rout, the S&P 500 remains near the all-time highs it set earlier this month.
A major sell-off in French government debt has also dragged European stocks lower in recent weeks.
But a significant market drawdown in the United States threatens to further dent Republicans’ prospects in the upcoming midterm elections.
President Donald Trump frequently points to solid stock market gains as evidence that his economic agenda has made Americans richer.
A prolonged market stumble ahead of the Nov. 3 elections would undermine this core argument for Trump and the GOP.

articles.title_zh: Oracle Stock Was Caught In the AI Debt Selloff. That Could Be a Mistake.
articles.content_orig:
Oracle, the multinational tech giant has taken on a lot of loans to build up its AI capacity. But Oracle's investors are not happy with this piling debt load.
Tech giant Oracle has added a lot of debt lately, which is drawing questions from Wall Street investors. Our colleagues Rick Mulvey and Adrian Ma at The Indicator explain how Oracle's fortunes and the AI boom connect to the wider economy.
ADRIAN MA, BYLINE: Oracle is one of those companies that you've probably heard of but may not deal with directly. It's a multinational tech giant that sells enterprise software and computing power.
RICKY MULVEY, BYLINE: Yeah. The vast majority of big companies use its databases and software.
MA: And about a decade ago, credit analysts viewed Oracle bonds as a safe investment.
MATT SHERIDAN: They were a high-margin software company. Now they're a capital-intensive data center buildout? This was a huge shift.
MA: Matt Sheridan is a senior lecturer in the finance department at...
SHERIDAN: The Ohio State University.
MULVEY: Matt analyzed credit before working as a professor too.
SHERIDAN: The biggest issue with Oracle is that load has nearly doubled in the last two years. They're sitting at 169 billion in total debt.
MA: Oracle went into the AI boom in a weaker financial spot than other tech giants.
MULVEY: Larry Ellison is the co-founder, executive chairman at Oracle. He thinks that training AI models is a huge business opportunity.
MA: So why aren't Oracle investors happy?
MULVEY: One reason is the sheer size of the debt. It's turned Oracle from a business that generates cash into one that burns money.
MA: Another is that the path back to profitability may take some time. Building data centers takes a second.
MULVEY: Oracle is relying on OpenAI a lot. Sam Altman and the folks at OpenAI promised Oracle they would pay about $300 billion over the next five or so years. Oracle's data centers help power ChatGPT.
MA: And OpenAI's financials come with a lot of open questions, mostly because you probably can't see them.
MULVEY: And Matt says if OpenAI's financials were out in the open, its value would also be based on its actual numbers.
SHERIDAN: So if you can't really trust that OpenAI's revenues are going to be growing at parabolic speed, that trickles into Oracle.
MA: Oracle and OpenAI are not just in a customer-seller relationship. This bit has more implications for the wider economy.
MULVEY: OpenAI pays Oracle to use its cloud infrastructure and says it'll pay a lot more in the coming years. So Oracle buys chips from Nvidia to build this cloud even more. And then Nvidia invests money into OpenAI so that OpenAI can buy computing space from Oracle, which, remember, is buying those Nvidia chips.
MA: I'm just picturing a circle. And according to credit investors, Oracle is a weak link in this circular economy.
MULVEY: Oracle has already signaled that it may run into trouble paying back its loans on time. This notice created some alarming headlines, but Matt says it actually could benefit Oracle. It allows the company to delay payments, though it's still on the hook for the full amount.
MA: Still, Oracle's credit investors are pricing in more risk. S&P, the big credit rating agency - they downgraded Oracle's credit in July. Now Oracle is barely above junk status. Matt says these circular deals and heavy amounts of debt could lead to real problems for the economy as a whole.
SHERIDAN: And that makes me concerned that if this is a bubble, it's going to be more like a Lehman Brothers-type event. And they're all becoming very interconnected.
MA: For now, the wheel is still turning.
